title: Example 2: Iodine clock reaction
summary: The iodine clock reaction studies a reaction too fast to observe by adding a small fixed amount of S2O3^2-(aq) and starch. I2 produced by reaction (1) is consumed immediately by S2O3^2- (reaction 2), so the solution stays clear until all S2O3^2- is used up. Then free I2 forms a dark blue complex with starch (reaction 3), giving a sudden colour change that marks the time.

blocks.text: Example 2: Determining initial rates in iodine clock reaction.
The iodine clock reaction is commonly used to study the rate of reaction. Consider the following reaction.
Red: too fast -> can't record the appearance of brown I2

Rate can be studied by introducing a small and fixed amount of S2O3^2-(aq) and starch indicator. Once I2(aq) is produced from reaction (1), it is consumed immediately by the added S2O3^2-(aq), reaction (2).
However, when all the added S2O3^2-(aq) has been consumed, any free I2(aq) immediately forms a dark blue complex with the starch indicator.
I2(aq) + starch -> dark blue complex   reaction (3)
Red bracket on reactions: slow down the observation

Time arrow over three beakers left to right. Beaker 1: H2O2 being added (arrow down), solution contains H+, I-, S2O3^2-, Starch; label 'Clear solution'. Beaker 2: H2O2, I-, H+, S2O3^2- + I2 (curved arrow), Starch; label 'Clear solution'. Beaker 3: solution dark; S2O3^2- crossed out, H2O2, I-, H+, I2 + Starch; label 'Dark blue solution'.
Summary below beakers: H2O2(aq) + 2I-(aq) + 2H+(aq) -> I2(aq) + 2H2O(l); 2S2O3^2-(aq) + I2(aq) -> S4O6^2-(aq) + 2I-(aq); I2(aq) + starch -> dark blue complex

key_concepts: S2O3^2- consumes I2 immediately (reaction 2), keeping the solution clear
Starch indicator forms a dark blue complex with free I2 (reaction 3) once all S2O3^2- is consumed
Sudden colour change marks a measurable time; fixed small amount of S2O3^2- slows down the observation

animation.concept: S2O3^2- silently mops up I2 as it forms; only when S2O3^2- runs out does I2 accumulate and the solution suddenly turns dark blue with starch.
animation.why: The key insight is a particle-level competition that produces a delayed, abrupt colour change. A 3D beaker with particles shows the consumption of S2O3^2- and the sudden change far better than the static three-beaker picture.

steps.visual: A transparent glass cylinder beaker (open top) filled with pale, clear liquid (a translucent box/cylinder). Inside float labelled particles: 6 H+ (small white spheres), 6 I- (light grey-blue spheres), 6 S2O3^2- (orange spheres), and 2 starch rods (small flat cream-coloured capsules). Particles jiggle randomly. Counter sprite 'S2O3^2- left: 6'.
steps.caption: Clear solution: H+, I-, S2O3^2- and starch

steps.visual: A large H2O2 sphere (blue-white, label) descends from above through the beaker mouth; then 6 H2O2 spheres spread in the liquid. Equation sprite for reaction (1) appears at the side.
steps.caption: H2O2 added: reaction (1) starts

steps.visual: Repeatedly (about every 1.5 s, 5 events): an H2O2 + 2 I- + 2 H+ cluster merges and a brown I2 sphere (larger, brown) appears; within 0.5 s it collides with an S2O3^2- pair (two orange spheres), and all three turn into S4O6^2- (one yellow-green sphere) plus two I- (grey-blue) returning to the pool. Liquid stays clear. Counter 'S2O3^2- left' drops 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Equation (2) highlights.
steps.caption: S2O3^2- consumes I2 immediately: reaction (2)

steps.visual: Final S2O3^2- spheres reach zero; the last orange sphere is shown crossed out by a red X and disappears. Counter reads 'S2O3^2- left: 0'. Liquid still clear for a brief pause. A stopwatch sprite near the beaker reaches its stop moment.
steps.caption: All the added S2O3^2- has been consumed

steps.visual: A new brown I2 sphere forms (reaction 1) and, with nothing left to consume it, stays. It approaches a starch capsule and docks to it (I2 + starch). At that instant the liquid colour animates from clear to dark navy blue within about 0.4 s (sudden, not gradual).
steps.caption: Free I2 + starch -> dark blue complex: reaction (3)

steps.visual: The dark blue solution stays; more I2 spheres dock onto starch (blue-black complexes). The stopwatch freezes and is labelled 't = time for dark blue to appear'. The three equations (1), (2), (3) stack at the side with the one currently relevant highlighted.
steps.caption: Sudden dark blue marks the end of the 'clock'

steps.visual: Camera pulls back to show three small copies of the beaker in a row labelled with the book's stages: Clear solution, Clear solution, Dark blue solution, with a 'Time' arrow above. Then fade and loop.
steps.caption: Clear -> clear -> dark blue as time passes

elements: transparent beaker (open cylinder) with liquid cylinder whose colour/opacity animates clear -> dark navy
particle spheres: H+, I-, S2O3^2-, H2O2, I2 (brown), S4O6^2-
text sprite labels on particles (H2O2, H+, I-, S2O3^2-, Starch, I2)
red X over the last S2O3^2-
Time arrow plane/line with three mini beakers
correctness_notes: Reaction (2): 2S2O3^2- + I2 -> S4O6^2- + 2I-; each I2 consumes TWO S2O3^2-, and I- is regenerated
Reaction (3): I2 + starch -> dark blue complex; this only happens once ALL the added S2O3^2- is consumed
The solution must stay clear/colourless until S2O3^2- is used up, then change suddenly; do not fade gradually
The page's handwriting says the reaction (1) alone is too fast to record the brown I2 appearance, so S2O3^2- and starch slow down the observation
S2O3^2- is a small FIXED amount, so the time to blue is a stopwatch for reaction (1)
